content: Glossitis refers to the inflammation or infection of the tongue. This condition can cause the tongue to swell and change in color. The finger-like projections on the tongue's surface, known as papillae, may be lost, resulting in a smooth appearance of the tongue. Glossitis typically responds well to treatment if the underlying cause of the inflammation is addressed. The condition may be painless, but it can also lead to discomfort in the tongue and mouth. In severe cases, glossitis can cause significant tongue swelling that obstructs the airway, which constitutes a medical emergency requiring immediate attention. Causes Common Causes: Alcohol consumption Benign migratory glossitis Use of medications like deserpidine or reserpine Erythema multiforme Folate deficiency Glucagonoma Iron deficiency Lichen planus Malnutrition Pellagra Pernicious anemia Spices Xerostomia (dry mouth) Causes by Organ System: Glossitis can result from a variety of systemic or localized conditions, including: AIDS Alcoholism Allergic reactions Anemia Angular cheilitis Aphthous ulcers Ariboflavinosis Candidiasis Celiac disease Crohn’s disease Dehydration Deficiencies in vitamins such as niacin, riboflavin, thiamine, or pyridoxine Iron deficiency anemia Kawasaki disease Lichen planus Malnutrition Oral lichen planus Pemphigus vulgaris Pernicious anemia Poor oral hygiene Psoriasis Smoking Syphilis Trauma or mechanical irritation Xerostomia Zinc deficiency Certain medications, such as doxycycline, lincomycin hydrochloride, meropenem, and tetracycline, can also contribute to glossitis. Symptoms Swelling of the tongue A smooth appearance of the tongue due to the loss of papillae Changes in tongue color, often appearing dark beefy red. In cases of pernicious anemia, the tongue may appear pale, while deficiencies in B vitamins can cause a fiery red color. Soreness and tenderness of the tongue Difficulty with chewing, swallowing, or speaking If symptoms persist for more than 10 days, or if severe tongue swelling interferes with breathing, speaking, chewing, or swallowing, a healthcare provider should be consulted immediately. Causes, Incidence, and Risk Factors Glossitis can be caused by bacterial or viral infections, including oral herpes simplex. Poor hydration and low saliva production can create an environment conducive to bacterial growth. Mechanical irritation or injury, such as burns, rough edges of teeth, or dental appliances, can also lead to glossitis. Exposure to irritants like tobacco, alcohol, hot foods, or spices is another common cause. Allergic reactions to toothpaste, mouthwash, breath fresheners, dyes in candy, or materials in dentures or retainers can trigger glossitis. Certain blood-pressure medications, such as ACE inhibitors, may also contribute. Systemic disorders, including iron deficiency anemia, pernicious anemia, B-vitamin deficiencies, oral lichen planus, erythema multiforme, aphthous ulcers, pemphigus vulgaris, and syphilis, are associated with glossitis. In rare cases, glossitis may be inherited. A painful tongue may indicate serious underlying medical conditions and should be evaluated by a doctor or dentist. Treatment The primary goal of treatment is to reduce inflammation. Hospitalization is generally not required unless tongue swelling is severe. Good oral hygiene is essential, including thorough tooth brushing at least twice daily and daily flossing. Corticosteroids, such as prednisone, may be prescribed to reduce inflammation. For mild cases, topical applications like a prednisone mouth rinse (not swallowed) may be recommended to avoid systemic side effects. If an infection is the cause, antibiotics, antifungal medications, or other antimicrobials may be prescribed. Nutritional deficiencies, such as anemia, should be addressed through dietary changes or supplements. Avoiding irritants like hot or spicy foods, alcohol, and tobacco can help minimize discomfort. Prevention Maintaining good oral hygiene, including regular professional cleanings and examinations, can help prevent glossitis. Drinking plenty of water and ensuring adequate saliva production can reduce bacterial growth. Minimizing exposure to irritants or injuries in the mouth is also important. Avoid excessive consumption of foods or substances that may irritate the tongue or mouth.
